questions.problem: Calculate $\int \frac{1}{5-2x}\,\text{d}x.$ Assume that $K$ is an arbitrary positive constant.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let $u=5-2x.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2\,⟹\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

We can now rewrite the integral in terms of $u,$ solve it, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{5-2x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot (-\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|5-2x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

We can further simplify the above by writing $C=-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡K$ for another arbitrary constant $K,$ and then we can combine the two terms using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|5-2x|+C & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|5-2x|-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡K \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡|5-2x|+\operatorname{ln}⁡K) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|5-2x|)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we finally conclude that

$$
\int \frac{1}{5-2x}\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|5-2x|).
$$

questions.problem: Calculate $\int (\frac{1}{x+3}+\frac{1}{x-3})\,\text{d}x.$ Assume that $K$ is an arbitrary positive constant.
questions.worked_solution:
Let's solve this using the general formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (\frac{1}{x+3}+\frac{1}{x-3})\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{x+3}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{x-3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+3|+\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-3|+C \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|(x+3)(x-3)|+\operatorname{ln}⁡K \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|(x+3)(x-3)|)\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we used the laws of logarithms to write the result as a single logarithm.

$$

canonical_examples.problem: Calculate $\displaystyle{\int \dfrac{1}{1+2x}\textrm{d}x},$ writing your final answer as a single function.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, let $u=1+2x.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = 2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d x = \dfrac 1 2 \textrm d u.
$$

We can now rewrite the integral in terms of $u,$ solve it, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{1+2x}\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|1+2x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

We can further simplify the above by writing $C = \dfrac 1 2\ln K$ for another arbitrary constant $K > 0,$ and then we can combine the two terms using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|1+2x|+C & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|1+2x|+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡K \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(K\cdot |1+2x|) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|1+2x|)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we finally conclude that

$$
\int \dfrac{1}{1+2x}\textrm{d}x  = \dfrac 1 2 \ln \left(K |1+2x|\right).
$$
